blocks.text: From this it might seem possible to conclude that doves have nested in Syria as well as in Greece from all time. Yet there is an objection to be raised: in the age of Moses, it is true, בני יונה, young of doves, were offered even by common people in Israel, as the Law expressly prescribes; but whether Abraham offered the same can be called into question. For we do not read that he offered תור ובן יונה, a turtledove and a young dove, as is commanded [II, 531] in the Law of Moses, but תור וגוזל, a turtledove and a gozal. This word signifies not only the young of the dove properly so called, but also the young of the turtledove, of the wood pigeon, of the livia, of the vinago, and of any other bird that may be assigned to the dove kind. Damir, in the chapter On القطا [al-qaṭā] alkata, as the Arabs call a certain kind of wood pigeon, writes: يقال القطا والحمام وانواعها امهات الجوازل والجوازل فراخها الواحد جوزل [yuqāl al-qaṭā wa-l-ḥamām wa-anwāʿuhā ummahāt al-jawāzil wa-l-jawāzil firākhuhā al-wāḥid jawzal] "Alkata and the dove, and [col. 7] birds of the same kind are called the mothers of the algavvazil. And the algavvazil are their young, from the singular gauzal." Now جوزل [jawzal] gauzal is for the Arabs exactly what גוזל gozal is for the Hebrews. Accordingly, since there are various species of gozal, when a pipio [squab] is meant precisely, there is sometimes added, by way of distinction, "gozal, young of the dove." Thus in the Chaldee paraphrast of the Song of Songs, chapter 1, verse 15: "Your eyes are כגוזלין בני יונתא, like gozalin, young of the dove." And Vajikra Rabba, chapter 22, on the emperor Titus: קראו לרופאים ומצאו בו כמו גוזל בן יונה והיה בו משקל שתי לטראות, "They called the physicians, who (when his skull had been cut open) found in it something like a gozal, a young of the dove, weighing two pounds." It is called gozal, or gauzal, from its peeping, just as in Latin pipio. For الجزل [al-jazl] algezel is pipitus [peeping]. In the Alcamus it is rendered صوت الحمام [ṣawt al-ḥamām] the voice of the dove, namely of one still peeping and not yet grown. Therefore those are mistaken who derive גוזל gozal from the verb גזל gazal, that is, to seize, because it is exposed to plunder. The Syrians, by metathesis, say ܙܘܓܠ zogal instead of ܓܘܙܠ gozal. But the Phoenicians of old said gozol. Hence peristereon is in Punic חציר־גוזול azirgozol, that is, herb of the squab, in the Herbarium of Apuleius, chapter 65.
